message_content: What are the main mission goals and scientific outcomes you want this telemetry processing effort to support, in practical terms?

In practical terms, we want to turn the raw spacecraft telemetry into reliable science-ready data products that let the ASPERA-3 team study the particle and field environment around Mars, especially how the solar wind interacts with the Martian atmosphere and space environment. The processing effort should preserve the full mission record, so scientists can reanalyze it later with improved methods if needed, and it should also make recent results available quickly enough for day-to-day mission and science use. We also want the validated products to be suitable for long-term archiving, so the data remain usable well after the mission operations phase.
What primary science objectives should the ground system support beyond processing and preserving the particle and field telemetry?

Beyond basic processing and preservation, the ground system should support science use of the data for understanding the plasma environment around Mars and how it changes over time. In practice, that means making the products good enough for the team to analyze particle populations, fields, and interactions with the solar wind, and to compare different time periods or events. It should also support publication-quality analysis and later reprocessing if the science team refines the calibration or interpretation.

Looking at the mission context, what assumptions should we make about when and how the science team and other users will need access to these data over the mission life, and what level of availability do they expect from the ground system?

We should assume the science team will need access continuously throughout the mission, not just during routine operations, because they’ll be doing ongoing analysis, checking recent data, and revisiting older events as new questions come up. They’ll likely expect the system to make recent products available fairly quickly after acquisition, while also keeping the historical record accessible for the full mission lifetime and beyond through the archive. I’d also assume the public-facing recent data can tolerate a little more delay than the internal science products, but the operational side still needs to be dependable and available most of the time.
Which specific spacecraft data sources and ASPERA-3 instrument types do we need to support in the ground system?

We need to support the telemetry coming from the ASPERA-3 particle and field instruments themselves, along with the related spacecraft housekeeping data that’s needed to interpret and calibrate those measurements. I don’t have the full instrument list memorized at this level, so I’d want to verify the exact ASPERA-3 sensor types with the science team before locking that down. At a minimum, though, the system has to handle the instrument science packets and the supporting ancillary data needed for processing.

Are there any mission phases, outages, or access constraints when the science team would not need or expect continuous availability, or should we assume they need dependable access to recent and historical data at all times throughout the mission?

We should assume they want dependable access to both recent and historical data essentially all the time throughout the mission. There may be brief outages for maintenance or processing interruptions, but those should be exceptions, not something the team plans around. For requirements purposes, I’d treat continuous access as the expectation and then allow for short, well-communicated downtime if needed.

When you use the mission name and product names in practice, what terms or naming conventions should the ground system follow so users can clearly tell what each item is and how it fits into the mission?

We should use the mission and instrument names consistently, so users can immediately recognize ASPERA-3 data and distinguish it from other Mars Express products if needed. Product names should make it clear whether something is raw, processed, validated, or archive-ready, and ideally indicate the relevant instrument or data level in a predictable way. I’d expect the team to prefer stable naming conventions that are easy to sort, search, and cite in publications.

When the ground system receives spacecraft data for ingestion, what should it do if some packets are missing or the data set is only partially complete—accept it as-is, hold it for later completion, or handle it another way?

It should accept partial data if that’s all that arrives, because we can’t always wait for a perfectly complete set in mission operations. The important thing is to flag missing packets or gaps clearly in the processed output so scientists know what is complete and what is not. If late data turns up later, the system should be able to incorporate it and regenerate the affected products rather than treating the first version as final.
How should the system handle the mission’s expected data volume and processing load over time, including any periods when intake or storage needs may spike beyond the usual day-to-day level?

We should design it to handle normal daily throughput comfortably, but also to absorb spikes without losing data or backing up the whole pipeline. Those spikes could happen during periods of higher mission activity, when reprocessing is triggered, or if a backlog builds up after an outage. I’d expect the system to queue work and scale storage and processing headroom enough that peak loads don’t interrupt ingestion or delay the critical science products too much.
Under what conditions should the system stop product creation altogether rather than generate a degraded or partial product?

If the input data are so incomplete or corrupted that the result would be scientifically misleading, then it should stop and not publish a product. The same applies if a required calibration, ancillary file, or processing step is missing and we can’t produce something trustworthy. In those cases, it’s better to fail clearly and alert the team than to create an output that looks valid but isn’t.

When partial telemetry is accepted, should the processing workflow continue downstream immediately, or are there specific checks or minimum thresholds it must pass before generating analysis-ready products?

It should not push everything downstream immediately without checks. I’d expect at least basic completeness, integrity, and consistency checks before anything is turned into analysis-ready product, and if the data fall below a minimum threshold the workflow should hold or mark it as incomplete. The exact threshold probably depends on the product type, so I’d want that defined per processing step rather than one blanket rule.

For the checks before product creation, how do the minimum thresholds vary by processing step or product type—for example, what specific completeness, integrity, or consistency conditions would cause a step to hold the workflow or mark the output incomplete?

That varies by product level and by what the science users need from it. For the more basic products, we can tolerate some missing telemetry as long as the packet structure is intact and the gaps are clearly identified, but for analysis-ready products we need the key measurements, time tags, and calibration context to be consistent enough that the results are scientifically usable. If a step depends on a housekeeping stream, an attitude file, or a calibration table and that dependency is missing or obviously out of sync, I’d expect the workflow to hold or flag the output as incomplete rather than quietly continuing.

When a telemetry or processing failure occurs, what should trigger operator intervention versus automatic retry or holding the workflow, and how should the system escalate it if the issue cannot be resolved automatically?

If it looks like a transient ingestion or transfer problem, the system should retry automatically a few times and then hold the workflow if it still fails. Operator intervention is needed when the failure is persistent, affects the integrity of the product, or points to a missing external dependency that the system cannot recover on its own. If it can’t be resolved automatically, it should raise a clear alert to the operations team with enough context to see what failed, what data are affected, and whether anything was already partially processed.
Which channels should be authorized for the science team to receive processed products, such as a project data system, shared workspace, or direct file delivery?

The main channel should be the project’s own data system, since that’s the controlled place the science team will trust for validated products and reprocessing history. A shared workspace is useful for working copies, quick-look items, or internal review, but I wouldn’t want that to be the primary archive path. Direct file delivery can be supported as a convenience for specific users or transfers, but the authoritative distribution should stay centered on the project data system.
What is the primary way science team members should access and retrieve products from the project data system in their day-to-day work?

They should primarily use a web-based project portal or similar authenticated interface for day-to-day retrieval. That gives them a consistent way to search, browse, and download the products without having to rely on manual file exchanges. If needed, we could also support scripted or programmatic access for advanced users, but the portal should be the main route.

Are there any specific transfer protocols, interface standards, or destination-specific constraints that should govern how products move between the mission systems, user portal, and archive destination, such as limits on file format, timing, authentication, or allowed transfer methods?

Yes, there should be some controls, especially around authentication and file format. The mission systems and portal should use secure transfer methods, and the archive delivery has to follow whatever format and packaging rules the archive provider requires, since that destination is usually the most constrained. I don’t know the exact protocol names or timing limits yet, but I’d expect those to be defined by the interfaces we already have to support rather than left open-ended.

What are the main business reasons for these transfer and archive constraints, and in practice where do you expect the strictest operational limits to apply across the mission systems, portal, and archive delivery?

The main reasons are data integrity, traceability, and making sure the products can actually be accepted and preserved by the archive without rework. In practice, the strictest limits will be at the archive delivery point, because that side usually dictates the required packaging, metadata, and validation rules, while the portal and internal mission interfaces can be a bit more flexible as long as they stay secure and consistent. The mission systems also need to be reliable, but I’d expect fewer externally imposed constraints there than at the archive boundary.

What operational environment or hosting setup should we assume for the mission systems, portal, and archive delivery—such as on-premises, cloud, or a mixed environment—and are there any business rules about where the products or supporting services must or must not be hosted?

I’d assume a mixed environment unless we’re told otherwise. The mission systems and the archive delivery path are more likely to stay in controlled institutional or partner infrastructure, while the portal could potentially be hosted where it’s easiest to support secure access and availability. I’m not aware of any hard business rule yet that forbids cloud use, but anything handling flight-derived data or archive submissions would need to meet the project’s security and preservation requirements.
What specific recent information should be made publicly viewable—for example, raw telemetry, processed science data, status summaries, or another subset?

It should be a limited, curated subset rather than raw telemetry. I’d expect recent status summaries, quick-look or preliminary science products, and possibly some basic mission or instrument health information that’s safe to publish. Anything not yet validated or anything sensitive should stay out of the public view until it’s approved.

Are there any specific filtering or redaction rules for the public subset, such as removing certain fields, masking sensitive values, or withholding items until they meet validation or approval criteria?

Yes, the public subset should be filtered so only approved, non-sensitive information is exposed. We’d want to withhold anything that isn’t validated yet, and strip out fields that could be misleading or operationally sensitive, even if they’re not strictly confidential. The exact redaction rules would need to be defined with the science and operations teams, because I don’t know all the details offhand.
What should the public experience be like when someone views these approved updates, and are there any accessibility expectations or audience needs that should shape how the information is presented?

It should be simple and easy to understand for a general audience, not just specialists. The updates should load quickly, be readable on standard browsers and mobile devices, and present the latest approved information in a clean way with enough context to make it meaningful. Accessibility should be taken seriously, so we should assume basic web accessibility expectations like readable contrast, keyboard use, and screen-reader support.
For telemetry and science data, are there any business rules about how granular the records should be, or when data should be grouped into files or bundles versus kept as individual items?

Yes, the granularity should follow the operational and scientific use case. Telemetry is usually better handled in time-ordered chunks or packets that preserve the original sequence, while science data can be grouped into products or bundles that make analysis and archiving easier. I’d expect the exact bundling rules to depend on the instrument and the downstream archive requirements, so we shouldn’t force a one-size-fits-all approach.

When late spacecraft data arrives after an initial partial ingestion, what should the system do with the affected products—such as whether to automatically regenerate them, preserve earlier versions, or notify users in a specific way?

If late data arrives, the affected products should be regenerated automatically if possible, because we want the delivered science and archive products to stay complete and consistent. We should preserve the earlier version for traceability, at least internally, so we can tell what changed and when. Users who already received the older product should be notified if the update is significant enough to affect analysis, but I’d expect that notification policy to be tied to the product type and how material the change is.

For the ingestion pipeline itself, when spacecraft data arrives incomplete, do you want it to be accepted and processed as partial input with the gaps clearly marked, or should that remain an undecided rule for now?

I’d lean toward accepting it as partial input rather than rejecting it outright, as long as the missing portions are clearly marked and the downstream products reflect that incompleteness. That keeps the pipeline moving and gives operations something usable instead of waiting indefinitely. But if the gaps make a product scientifically unreliable, then that specific product should probably stay flagged or held back until the missing data arrives.

Under what conditions should users be notified about a regenerated product update, and how do you want to distinguish between changes that are merely informational versus changes significant enough to affect analysis?

Users should be notified when the regeneration changes the actual science content, time coverage, calibration, or any quality flag that could alter how the product is interpreted. Purely operational changes, like reformatting or internal processing cleanup that do not affect the results, would usually be informational only and probably not worth a direct notice. If the difference could change someone’s conclusions or require them to re-run analysis, then it should be treated as significant.

How should regenerated products be distributed to users who already received an earlier version—should they be automatically replaced, made available as a new version for re-download, or handled differently depending on the product type or user group?

They should be available as a new version rather than silently replacing the earlier one, so users can see the history and compare if needed. For active project team users, we’d want the new version to be pushed or prominently flagged, but for archived or public users it can just be published as the revised product with clear versioning. I do think the handling can vary a bit by product type, especially if something is preliminary versus validated.
For the cases where product type changes the handling, what concrete rule should decide whether a new version is just published with versioning or actively pushed and flagged to users?

If the product is still within the active science or operations workflow, then it should be actively pushed and flagged. If it’s a validated or archival product that has already been formally delivered, then it should just be published as a new version with clear versioning and a record of what changed. The main dividing line is whether people are expected to be using it right now for current work or whether it’s already part of the preserved record.

For ground system users, are there any cases where a regenerated product should be both pushed and versioned differently depending on the user group, or should the distribution rule change only by whether the product is still actively in use versus part of the preserved record?

I’d keep the main rule based on whether the product is actively in use versus part of the preserved record. That said, the way we push or flag it can differ by user group, because the project team may need an immediate alert while broader users may only need the new version made available. So the versioning should stay consistent, but the notification and delivery urgency can be tailored to the audience.

When defining the archive package, are there any rules for how the mission, instrument, and product names should appear together in the package hierarchy or file names so the validated delivery stays easy to identify and distinguish from other Mars Express holdings?

Yes, we should make the archive naming clearly reflect the mission, the ASPERA-3 instrument, and the product type so it is unambiguous in the Mars Express holdings. I’d expect the hierarchy and filenames to be consistent and human-readable, with the validated delivery standing out from any working or preliminary products. I don’t know that we have a finalized naming convention yet, but the rule should be that someone can identify the dataset and its maturity level without opening the files.

How should the archive package name and folder structure signal special cases such as reprocessed deliveries, corrected products, or superseded versions so users can tell which package is the current preserved record?

Those special cases should be signaled very explicitly in the versioning and status labels, not hidden in vague naming. The current preserved record ought to be the one marked as the active validated version, while reprocessed or corrected deliveries should carry clear revision identifiers and a status that shows they supersede an earlier package. If there are multiple retained versions, the folder structure should make the chronological and authority order obvious so users can tell which one they should trust.

For the operational hosting of the mission systems, portal, and archive delivery path, are there any component-specific rules or boundary conditions that determine where each part must run, such as if one environment is required for security, preservation, or access reasons while others can be hosted more flexibly?

Yes, there are boundary conditions, but I would separate them by function. The archive delivery and preservation functions need to be in a controlled environment with strong integrity and retention protections, while the public portal can be hosted more flexibly as long as it only exposes approved recent information. The operational processing side should stay close to the controlled mission data flow so we can protect incoming telemetry and keep the chain of custody clear.

Are there any business rules or operational conditions for the persistent identifiers and catalog fields in the archive package—such as when they must remain stable across reprocessed or corrected deliveries, or when a new identifier or catalog entry should be assigned?

Yes, the persistent identifiers should stay stable for the same science product lineage, even if it gets reprocessed or corrected, so users and archives can trace it over time. A new identifier or catalog entry should only be assigned when the content is truly a different product family or a distinct deliverable, not just a revision of the same one. The catalog should also preserve the relationship between superseded and current versions so the history is unambiguous.

For the ASPERA-3 instrument types, are there any practical rules or exceptions we should apply in the archive when one sensor stream is missing, combined, or represented only through housekeeping or ancillary data rather than direct science packets?

Yes, there should be a practical rule that the archive still records whatever valid data exists, even if one sensor stream is missing or only ancillary information is available. In those cases, the package should make it explicit that the delivery is partial or substituted, so users know they are not getting a full science stream. If streams are combined, we should preserve the provenance so it is clear which sensor sources contributed and which ones were absent.
Which exact ASPERA-3 sensor or instrument types do you want us to record now, and which ones should remain explicitly marked as undecided or tentative until the science team confirms them?

I can’t name the exact sensor list confidently without checking with the science team. What we do know is that the archive should support the ASPERA-3 particle and field instrument products we are actually receiving, and anything beyond that should stay marked as tentative until confirmed. For now, I’d rather not hard-code a sensor taxonomy that might turn out to be wrong later.

What operational rule should we use to decide whether incoming ASPERA-3 data should be kept as packet-level telemetry versus combined into science bundles, especially when mixed or borderline data types are delivered together?

The main rule should be to preserve the original packet-level telemetry whenever that is what arrives, and then build science bundles as derived products for analysis and distribution. If mixed or borderline data come in together, we should keep the raw packets intact and only bundle the parts that can be cleanly validated into a science product. That way we don’t lose provenance, and we can still support both detailed reprocessing and easier scientific use.
Which exact ASPERA-3 sensor types should the archive recognize as valid for this mission, including any that need to be treated as provisional until the science team confirms them?

I can’t give you an exact validated sensor list right now, because I don’t have that confirmed from the science team. The safe approach is to let the archive recognize the ASPERA-3 instrument products we know are in scope, but flag any sensor type not explicitly approved as provisional until the team signs off. That avoids locking us into an incorrect mission taxonomy too early.

When a sensor type is still provisional, what specific archive behavior do you want for its products—such as how they should be labeled, whether they should be included in validated deliveries or held back, and what changes once the science team approves them?

Provisional products should be clearly labeled as unvalidated or tentative, and I would keep them out of the validated delivery set until the science team approves them. They can still exist in the archive for internal review and traceability, but they should not be treated as final scientific products or pushed into the long-term validated package. Once approved, we would update the status and then include them in the normal validated delivery and archiving flow.
Are there any legal or contractual restrictions that would require certain archive holdings or disseminations to be withheld, delayed, redacted, or limited in who can access them?

I’m not aware of any special restrictions beyond the normal mission and agency data handling rules, but I can’t say there are none without checking the current agreements. If there are proprietary or embargoed items, the archive would need to support access controls and delayed release for those holdings. For now, I’d treat that as an open point to verify with the project and any archive partners.

For any archive deliveries that are subject to partner or agency controls, what transfer protocol and timing rules should the interface enforce in practice—for example, which methods are acceptable and what conditions would justify delaying, batching, or expediting a transfer?

In practice, I’d want the interface to use whatever secure transfer method the partner archive requires and that we can operationally support, with authenticated and auditable delivery as the baseline. Timing should normally follow the agreed delivery schedule, but we could delay or batch transfers if a product set is incomplete, still under validation, or flagged for partner review. We would only expedite a transfer if there is an agreed operational need or a release deadline that both sides have already accepted.

What should the public page do when new information is not yet ready for release—should it hold back the update, show a placeholder or summary, or continue displaying the last approved information until the new content is cleared for public access?

It should keep displaying the last approved public information until the new content is cleared for release. I would not want it to show a placeholder that makes the page look broken or empty, and I’d rather avoid exposing anything provisional. If we need to indicate freshness, that can be done with a simple timestamp or status note without publishing the unreleased content itself.

What specific content categories or field types should the public subset redaction rules always exclude or mask when release-ready information is prepared, especially where something is incomplete, operationally sensitive, or could be misleading even if it is not confidential?

For the public subset, I’d always exclude anything that is still provisional, incomplete, or could be misread as a final science result, including raw packet details, internal quality flags, and operational troubleshooting notes. I would also mask any content that exposes spacecraft operations timing, partner-only identifiers, or anything that could be sensitive from a mission support standpoint even if it is not strictly confidential. The general rule should be to publish only stable, clearly interpreted information that won’t mislead a non-specialist viewer.
Would you like to define the public-subset redaction rules now, or should we record that ownership and rule detail as undecided for the moment?

Let’s record the ownership and the detailed redaction rules as undecided for the moment. We know the intent at a high level, but the exact rule set should be confirmed with the science and operations teams before we freeze it.
Which users or systems should receive the release notification, and through what channel or channels should it be sent when a significant update is published?

The release notification should go to the ASPERA-3 science team and any operational support systems that need to react to the update. I’d expect email and an internal system notification at minimum, and maybe a machine-readable feed if another system needs to pick it up automatically. We can refine the exact recipient list and channels once we know who depends on the release event.

For archived users, should they simply see the revised version with history available, or is there any different handling you want when an older archived copy has already been distributed or referenced?

They should generally see the revised version with version history available, so it’s clear what changed and when. If an older copy has already been distributed or cited, we should not silently replace it everywhere; instead, we need to preserve traceability and make the superseded status obvious. I’d want the archive to keep the old record accessible enough for provenance, while steering users to the current approved version.

For the machine-readable feed, do you want it to be a continuously available subscription channel, a pollable endpoint, or both, and are there any rules about when systems should use one versus the other?

Both would be best if we can support them. The subscription channel should be used for immediate notification of significant updates, while the pollable endpoint gives systems a fallback and a way to reconcile missed events. I’d expect critical consumers to subscribe if they can, and use polling as a backup or for periodic consistency checks.

When a telemetry or processing step fails, what should determine whether the system retries automatically, pauses for operator review, or escalates immediately—for example, the type of failure, the number of retry attempts, or the impact on downstream data?

The decision should depend first on the type of failure and then on whether the failure affects data integrity or just delays processing. If it looks transient, like a network hiccup or a temporary service outage, automatic retries make sense up to a small limit; if it’s a corruption, validation, or science-product quality issue, it should pause for operator review right away. Anything that could block downstream delivery for a significant period or threaten the archive record should escalate immediately.

What specific conditions or rules should govern when a validated product is eligible to move from operational processing into long-term archive holdings, especially if there are timing, completeness, or approval exceptions?

A product should move into long-term archive holdings only after it has passed validation, has a complete associated metadata record, and has been formally approved as release-ready. If there are missing inputs, unresolved anomalies, or an open review item, it should stay out of the archive until that is cleared. I’d also want any exception to require explicit sign-off, because once it’s in the archive it needs to be treated as a preserved scientific record.
Do you want to define any specific boundary conditions for the archive environment itself, or should we record that as undecided for now?

We should record that as undecided for now. I know the archive has to be durable and accessible for long-term preservation, but I don’t want to invent boundary conditions without checking the storage and mission operations expectations.
Which functions, if any, need to be hosted in a controlled environment to preserve chain of custody or data integrity, and which functions can remain more flexibly hosted?

Anything that acquires raw telemetry, performs validation, signs off products, or transfers data into the archive should be hosted in a controlled environment, because those are the points where integrity and provenance matter most. The public-facing recent-information service can be more flexibly hosted, as long as it only exposes approved information and doesn’t interfere with the controlled processing path. I’d also keep any administrative access to the archive tightly controlled.

Are there any conditions or exceptions under which a function that is normally near the controlled mission data flow could be hosted farther away from it, or must those functions always remain close to that controlled path?

There can be exceptions, but only if the function is clearly read-only or operates on already approved products and it still meets the integrity and access-control requirements. If it touches raw telemetry, validation state, or archive ingress, I would not want it moved farther away from the controlled path. For anything borderline, I’d expect a formal review and approval before allowing that separation.

When a science product is reprocessed or corrected, what operational rule should determine whether its persistent identifier and catalog entry remain the same or whether a new one is assigned, especially for superseded versus current versions?

If the reprocessing is just a correction or improved version of the same scientific product, I’d expect the persistent identifier and catalog entry to stay the same, with versioning used to show what changed. A new identifier should only be assigned if it’s effectively a different product line or a materially different dataset that shouldn’t be treated as a replacement. Superseded versions should remain traceable, but the current version needs to be clearly marked as the active one.

How would you describe the overall order of importance and handoff between ingestion, science processing, distribution, public access, and archive delivery in your mission, especially if one of those stages becomes a bottleneck or needs to be prioritized over the others?

Ingestion comes first and is the highest priority because if we don’t get the spacecraft data safely in, nothing else can happen. Science processing and archive delivery are next in line, since validated products need to be preserved and delivered reliably, while distribution to the project team should follow as soon as trustworthy products are available. Public access is important, but it should never take precedence over the controlled mission flow; if there’s a bottleneck, we would prioritize the raw data path, validation, and archive preservation before anything public-facing.
Are there any product features in this flow that you would treat as must-have for mission operations versus merely desirable if time and resources allow?

Yes, the must-haves are safe ingestion, validated processing, controlled handoff into archive holdings, and reliable delivery of the preserved products to the archive and the project team. Public viewing of recent information is desirable and part of the mission value, but I would treat it as secondary to the operational and preservation functions. Anything that improves usability or convenience beyond that would be nice to have, but not essential.

For the items you consider desirable rather than must-have, what operational conditions would make them worth enabling or deferring—for example, only after archive delivery is complete, only for public release, or only when they do not affect ingestion, validation, or preservation?

I’d only enable those desirable features when they cannot interfere with ingestion, validation, or preservation, and ideally after the operational products have been secured and handed off. Public release features are the clearest example, since they can wait until the mission-facing data path is stable and the approved content is ready. If there’s any risk of slowing down archive delivery or complicating traceability, I’d defer them.

When a product is being considered for archive admission, what specific conditions or review outcomes would cause you to hold it back from long-term archive holdings, or allow an exception with explicit sign-off?

I’d hold a product back if its provenance is unclear, if validation hasn’t completed, if the metadata is incomplete, or if there are unresolved quality issues that could mislead future users. An exception might be allowed only if the science team explicitly signs off that the product is still worth preserving, and that the limitation is documented so it’s not mistaken for a fully validated archive item. In that case, I’d still want it clearly labeled as provisional or nonstandard.

What practical archive-delivery constraints—such as packaging, metadata completeness, or validation at the handoff point—would make you send a processed product forward versus keep it in the operational system for rework?

I’d send it forward only when the package is complete, the metadata is sufficient for later discovery and use, and the validation results show it is fit for archive. If any of those are missing, I’d keep it in the operational system for rework rather than risk handing off something ambiguous or incomplete. The main idea is that once it crosses that handoff point, we should not expect to need operational fixes to make it usable later.
What retention period and preservation format, if any, do you expect for validated products once they enter long-term archive holdings?

For validated products, I would expect them to be retained indefinitely, or at least for the full scientific lifetime of the mission and beyond if the archive can support it. As for format, I’d prefer a stable, well-documented preservation format that is widely readable and not dependent on the operational processing environment. If we already have a community or agency archive standard, we should align with that rather than inventing something mission-specific.

When automatic recovery fails and operations must be alerted, what conditions should determine whether the issue is escalated immediately versus held for a short retry window, and what minimum context should the alert include for operations to act on it?

If the failure affects ingestion, could cause data loss, or blocks archive delivery, I’d escalate immediately. If it looks transient, like a brief connectivity or downstream service glitch, a short retry window is reasonable before paging operations. The alert should at minimum say what failed, when it failed, what data or product set is affected, how many retries have already happened, and whether any preservation risk is known.

When an alert does go out, are there any cases where you’d want different context included—such as the archive destination, severity of the preservation risk, or the specific retry stage reached—depending on whether the issue is at ingestion, processing, or delivery?

Yes, I’d want the context to vary by stage. For ingestion, the destination and whether any incoming telemetry is at risk would be most important; for processing, I’d want the failing step and which product versions are impacted; for delivery, I’d want the archive destination, the handoff status, and how serious the preservation risk is. The retry stage reached is useful in all cases, but it becomes especially important when we’re deciding whether to keep waiting or to escalate.

For the validated products you retain long term, what specific conditions or exceptions, if any, would allow the archive to place them under a finite retention limit or disposition them differently from the default indefinite retention approach?

The default should be indefinite retention for validated products, so I’d only accept a finite limit in unusual cases where policy or storage constraints make that unavoidable. If that happened, it would need explicit approval from the project and archive authorities, and the exception should be documented so we know exactly which products are affected and why. I would not want scientifically validated mission data discarded just because it is inconvenient to keep.

What practical conditions or operational thresholds would justify invoking that finite-retention exception for validated products, and how would you decide when storage pressure is serious enough to require it?

I’d only consider that if storage pressure becomes genuinely unsustainable and we have no practical expansion path, or if an external archive policy forces a different retention model. It would have to be more than routine capacity management; I’d expect repeated breaches of safe operating limits, with no near-term way to relieve them by cleanup, expansion, or re-tiering. Even then, I’d try very hard to preserve the validated products elsewhere before choosing disposal or a shorter retention period.

What operational event or escalation would make you say the storage pressure has crossed from serious strain into the point where the finite-retention exception must be activated, and who would be responsible for making that call?

That point would be when we’re at risk of failing archive acceptance or losing the ability to preserve newly validated products, not just when disks are getting full. If we’ve exhausted normal mitigation and the situation threatens mission data continuity, then the exception should be activated. I’d expect that call to be made by the project data management lead in coordination with archive operations, with project management signing off if it affects retention policy.

When the finite-retention exception is activated, what specific operational limits or approval steps govern who can authorize its use, and under what circumstances would that authority shift beyond the project data management lead and archive operations?

Normally, the project data management lead and archive operations should be enough to authorize the exception if they’re acting within an approved policy. If the exception would change the actual retention policy, affect contractual or agency obligations, or risk discarding validated science data, then that authority should shift up to project management and possibly the agency or archive governance chain. In practice, I’d want that escalation path documented ahead of time so nobody is improvising when the pressure is on.

When that escalation path is triggered, what specific decision owners should be responsible at each step, from the project data management lead and archive operations up through project management and any higher governance authority?

The project data management lead should own the technical recommendation, because they know the data flow, the retention impact, and the operational alternatives. Archive operations should confirm the archive-side constraints and whether any preservation workaround is possible. Project management should own the business and mission-risk decision, and any higher governance authority should only step in if the action changes formal retention commitments or external obligations.

Are there any conditions or boundary cases where the project data management lead and archive operations can authorize the storage-related action locally, or does it always have to be elevated to project management or higher once storage capacity is affected?

Yes, there are local cases where they can act without going higher, as long as it’s a routine operational response and doesn’t change the retention policy. For example, they could reallocate space, delay noncritical staging, or move products within approved storage tiers if that stays inside existing rules. Once the action would shorten retention, dispose of validated products, or create any policy exception, then it has to be elevated.

What operational trigger or boundary determines when a routine local storage action should stop being handled by the project data management lead and archive operations and instead be escalated for project management review?

The boundary is when the local action would have any irreversible impact or alter the approved preservation strategy. If it only buys time by reshuffling storage, that stays local; if it starts changing what gets kept, for how long, or at what scientific risk, then it needs project management review. I’d also escalate if the same workaround has to be used repeatedly, because that means the local fix is no longer really solving the problem.
When the same local storage workaround starts repeating, what specific sign or threshold tells you it’s time to stop treating it as a temporary fix and bring the issue into project management review?

I’d say it crosses that line when the workaround becomes part of the normal operating pattern rather than an occasional exception. If we’re repeating it often enough that it’s consuming staff time, delaying product delivery, or leaving us with no real buffer against the next data surge, then it should go to project management. At that point it’s a capacity or policy issue, not just an operational one.
